questions.stem: The heartland of the state of Qin lay in:
options: the Yangzi delta in the east, with ports on the coast
the far south, in the region of modern Guangzhou
the north-east, beyond the Yellow River near modern Beijing
the Wei River valley in the west, ringed by mountains
questions.explanation: Qin's base in the Wei valley was easy to defend and fertile once irrigated. Its western position also made it a frontier state used to warfare with non-Chinese peoples.

questions.stem: In the fourth century BCE Qin conquered Shu (in modern Sichuan), and the Dujiangyan irrigation works were later built there. Why did this matter for Qin's later conquests?
options: It allowed Qin to trade silk with Rome along the Silk Road
The Sichuan basin became a rich source of grain and a base against Chu
Sichuan's ports gave Qin a navy to attack Qi along the eastern coast
The region's horses gave Qin the only cavalry among the Warring States
questions.explanation: Irrigated Sichuan produced large grain surpluses to feed Qin's armies, and its position on the upper Yangzi threatened Chu from the west. The Silk Road to the Roman world opened much later.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Warring States period that Qin brought to an end in 221 BCE?
options: Seven major states fought for supremacy with large conscript armies
One Zhou king ruled all China through loyal nobles until Qin rebelled
Nomadic Xiongnu ruled northern China while the south stayed united
Two states, Qin and Chu, shared China under a lasting peace treaty
questions.explanation: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei competed in ever-larger wars, and the Zhou king had lost real power long before. The wars drove reforms in government, farming and the army.

questions.stem: In the fourth century BCE the minister Shang Yang reformed Qin. Which policy was part of his reforms?
options: Making Confucian scholars the judges in every county court
Ending conscription so that peasants could spend more time farming
Rank for military merit, and households grouped to report crime
Giving every noble family the right to raise its own private army
questions.explanation: Shang Yang tied rank to success in war and farming, organised households into groups held jointly responsible, and weakened the hereditary nobility. These Legalist measures made Qin a powerful war state.

questions.stem: The future First Emperor, named Zheng, was born in 259 BCE in Handan, capital of Zhao, because:
options: his grandfather had been exiled from Qin to Zhao
his father, a Qin prince, was a hostage there
his mother was a Zhao princess visiting her family
Qin had just conquered Zhao and moved its court there
questions.explanation: His father Zichu (later King Zhuangxiang) was a hostage in Zhao, a common guarantee between states. With Lu Buwei's help Zichu returned to Qin and became heir.

questions.stem: The Shiji reports a story that Zheng's real father was the merchant Lu Buwei, not Zichu. How do most historians treat this story?
options: As proven fact, since Lu Buwei admitted it in an inscription
As the reason Qin's nobles refused to accept him as king
As a story invented by modern scholars in the twentieth century
With caution, since it may reflect later hostility to the Qin ruler
questions.explanation: The story appears in Sima Qian's Han-era history and would have discredited the First Emperor's birth, so many scholars doubt it. There is no inscription proving it.

questions.stem: Zheng became king of Qin in 246 BCE:
options: after conquering Zhao and returning to Qin in triumph
as a boy of about thirteen, on his father's death
as a grown man of thirty, after defeating his brothers
after a vote of the Qin nobles at his father's funeral
questions.explanation: King Zhuangxiang died after a short reign, leaving Zheng king as a boy, so power was held at first by the chancellor Lu Buwei and the queen dowager.

questions.stem: During Zheng's minority, Lu Buwei was chancellor and regent. As well as running the government, he:
options: commanded the army that conquered every state except Qi
built the first stretches of the Great Wall along the Yellow River
wrote the Shiji as an official history of the Qin royal house
sponsored a large compendium of knowledge, the Lushi Chunqiu
questions.explanation: Lu Buwei gathered scholars to compile the Lushi Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn of Master Lu). The Shiji was written over a century later by Sima Qian.

questions.stem: In 238 BCE Lao Ai, a favourite of the queen dowager who had been made a marquis, attempted a coup. What followed?
options: The queen dowager became ruler and exiled Zheng to Zhao
Zheng crushed it, and Lu Buwei, Lao Ai's patron, was dismissed
Lao Ai ruled Qin as regent for five years until Zheng came of age
Lu Buwei led the coup and was made king of a separate state
questions.explanation: Zheng, now taking full power, defeated Lao Ai and had him executed. Lu Buwei, who had introduced Lao Ai to the court, was dismissed in 237 BCE, sent away and took his own life in 235.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about Zheng's early reign is best supported by the Lao Ai affair and the fall of Lu Buwei?
options: He acted decisively to remove rival centres of power once he ruled himself
He depended on the queen dowager's advice for the rest of his reign
He was a weak ruler controlled by his ministers until his death
He preferred to pardon his enemies in order to win their loyalty
questions.explanation: By destroying Lao Ai and removing Lu Buwei, the young king freed himself from the men who had dominated his minority. This ruthlessness anticipated his later style of rule.

questions.stem: Between 230 and 221 BCE Qin conquered the other six states. The last state to fall was:
options: Zhao
Chu
Qi
Han
questions.explanation: Han fell first in 230 BCE, followed by Zhao, Wei, Chu and Yan, and finally Qi in 221 BCE. Qi, in the far east, surrendered without a long fight.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains Qin's success in the wars of unification?
options: Its use of gunpowder weapons, which no other state possessed
An alliance with the Xiongnu, who attacked Qin's rivals from the north
The other states' refusal to fight because of Confucian pacifism
A centralised state that could mobilise men and grain on a huge scale
questions.explanation: Qin's Legalist system of conscription, rewards and grain production, built up since Shang Yang, let it wage long campaigns under generals such as Wang Jian. Gunpowder weapons came over a thousand years later.

questions.stem: After 221 BCE Zheng adopted new forms for his rule. Which of these was one of them?
options: He took the old Zhou title of 'king' and refused any new imperial title
He let each conquered state keep its own king as a loyal vassal
He made Confucius's descendants hereditary chancellors of the empire
He numbered rulers First Emperor, Second Emperor and so on
questions.explanation: He ruled that the dynasty would count its rulers as First Emperor, Second Emperor and so on, for ten thousand generations. He took the new title huangdi rather than wang (king).

questions.stem: The Shiji says Qin claimed to rule by the power of water, adopting black as its colour and six as its number. What was the purpose of this?
options: To present Qin as Zhou's rightful successor in the Five Phases
To honour the god of the Yellow River, whose temple Qin had founded
To show that Qin had conquered the coastal state of Qi by sea
To mark the beginning of a Buddhist calendar for the new empire
questions.explanation: In Five Phases theory each dynasty was linked to a phase, and water overcomes fire, the phase linked with Zhou. The symbolism presented the conquest as part of the natural order.

questions.stem: The Qin standardised the width of cart axles throughout the empire. The practical reason was that:
options: it allowed taxes to be counted by the number of axles owned
narrow axles were needed for carts crossing the Great Wall gates
it let Qin chariots fit the narrow mountain passes of Sichuan
carts could travel in the same ruts on roads in every region
questions.explanation: Roads, especially in loess country, wore deep ruts, so a single axle width let wagons move freely across the empire. It was part of a wider unification of measures.

questions.stem: The Qin standard round bronze coin with a square hole was called the:
options: banliang
wuzhu
bu (spade money)
dao (knife money)
questions.explanation: The banliang ('half ounce') replaced the spade, knife and other coins of the Warring States. The wuzhu coin was introduced later, under Emperor Wu of Han.

questions.stem: In 237 BCE Qin ordered the expulsion of foreign-born officials. Li Si, himself from Chu, wrote a memorial against the order, arguing that:
options: Qin had grown great by using able men from other states
foreign officials should be executed rather than expelled
only men born in Qin could be trusted to command the army
the king should return all conquered lands to their rulers
questions.explanation: Li Si pointed out that talented outsiders had served Qin well, and the order was withdrawn. He went on to become the chief minister of the empire.

questions.stem: In 213 BCE a scholar urged the emperor to give fiefs to his sons, as the Zhou had done. Li Si opposed this and proposed the burning of books. What linked his two positions?
options: Rejecting the past as a model, so scholars could not criticise the present
Protecting Confucian scholars from attacks by jealous Legalist officials at court
Saving money, since fiefs and libraries both cost the state a great deal
Preparing for war with the Xiongnu by sending all the princes to the frontier
questions.explanation: Li Si argued that scholars praised antiquity to attack current policy, so books of the old traditions outside official hands should be destroyed. Centralised commanderies, not fiefs, would keep power with the emperor.

questions.stem: Li Si and the philosopher Han Fei had both studied under Xunzi. According to the Shiji, when Han Fei came to Qin, he:
options: became chancellor and wrote the Qin legal code
led the conquest of his home state of Han
retired to teach Confucian texts in Xianyang
died in prison after Li Si spoke against him
questions.explanation: The Shiji says Li Si, fearing a rival, had Han Fei imprisoned and he died there in 233 BCE. Han Fei's writings, though, were admired by the king and shaped Legalist thought.

questions.stem: In each Qin commandery, authority was divided among a civil governor, a military commander and an imperial inspector. The purpose of this division was to:
options: let each commandery choose which of the three would rule it
ensure that Confucian scholars supervised military officers
stop any single official building a power base against the emperor
give local nobles a share of power in their own former kingdoms
questions.explanation: Splitting civil, military and supervisory roles and appointing officials from the centre kept the provinces dependent on the throne, unlike the hereditary fiefs of Zhou.

questions.stem: According to the Shiji, after unification the weapons of the empire were collected at Xianyang and melted down. What was done with the metal?
options: It was cast into bells and twelve giant bronze statues
It was minted into coins to pay the army on the frontier
It was used to make ploughs for the new state farms
It was buried in the emperor's tomb as an offering
questions.explanation: Disarming the conquered population reduced the risk of revolt, and turning the weapons into statues made a public show of peace under Qin.

questions.stem: Under the First Emperor, the general Meng Tian built the Straight Road (Zhidao). Its main purpose was to:
options: allow the emperor to reach his mausoleum during his lifetime
move troops fast from the capital to the northern frontier
carry silk from the capital to the markets of Central Asia
link the capital directly to the ports of the southern coast
questions.explanation: The Straight Road ran north from near Xianyang towards the Ordos and the frontier against the Xiongnu. It was part of a wider network of imperial highways.

questions.stem: During his tours of the empire, the First Emperor set up inscribed stone stelae on mountains such as Mount Tai and Langya. The inscriptions mainly:
options: gave instructions for the building of his mausoleum
praised his unification and the order his laws had brought
listed the names of the soldiers who died in the wars
recorded his apology for the burning of the books
questions.explanation: The stelae proclaimed the end of war, the unity of the empire and the emperor's virtue. The tours also showed imperial power in the newly conquered east.

questions.stem: The Lingqu canal, built in the south under the First Emperor, linked two river systems. Its main purpose was to:
options: water the farmland of the north China plain
supply Qin armies campaigning in the far south
drain the marshes around the capital at Xianyang
carry stone from Sichuan for the Great Wall
questions.explanation: By joining a tributary of the Yangzi to a river flowing south, the canal let grain and supplies reach the armies sent against the Yue peoples of the south.

questions.stem: The Shiji says replicas of the palaces of each conquered ruler were built near Xianyang, and a vast new palace, the Epang, was begun late in the reign. These projects best show that the emperor:
options: used building to show the old states absorbed into one empire
planned to return the conquered kings to their thrones after his death
wished to move his capital from Xianyang to the old state of Chu
spent nothing on building, as Legalist thought opposed it
questions.explanation: Recreating the palaces of defeated rulers at his capital displayed their subjection, and the Epang palace showed imperial grandeur. Such projects also demanded huge amounts of forced labour.

questions.stem: The 'Great Wall' of the Qin was mainly:
options: a single stone wall built from the coast to Central Asia
the brick wall seen today, completed by the First Emperor
a wall around the capital to keep out rebel armies
older walls of several states, joined and extended
questions.explanation: Meng Tian linked and extended the rammed-earth walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan against the Xiongnu. Most of the brick and stone wall seen today was built under the Ming dynasty.

questions.stem: The Shiji says the First Emperor sent the magician Xu Fu with young men and women across the eastern sea. The aim was to:
options: found trading colonies to sell silk to the Romans
find the islands of the immortals and the elixir of life
conquer Korea and add it to the empire's commanderies
bring back Buddhist teachers from India to the court
questions.explanation: The emperor was drawn to fangshi (magicians) who promised immortality, and Xu Fu reportedly never returned. The search reflects the emperor's fear of death.

questions.stem: Archaeologists have not opened the central mound of the First Emperor's mausoleum. Which reason do Chinese authorities and many archaeologists give?
options: Present methods cannot protect finds such as painted surfaces
The Shiji proves the tomb is empty, so excavation would be pointless
The mound is under a modern city that would have to be demolished
International law forbids the excavation of any royal tomb
questions.explanation: The paint on terracotta warriors flaked and faded soon after exposure, so archaeologists fear damage to organic and painted remains. Testing of the soil, not excavation, has been used to check Sima Qian's account.

questions.stem: Besides the terracotta army, pits around the First Emperor's mausoleum have revealed figures of officials and acrobats and two half-size bronze chariots. These finds suggest the mausoleum complex was meant to:
options: store weapons for a Qin army that would rise against the Han
serve as a public museum for visitors to the capital
honour the soldiers of the defeated states with burials
recreate his court and empire so he could rule in the afterlife
questions.explanation: The range of finds points to a whole imperial world, with entertainment and administration as well as an army, reflecting the belief that his power would continue after death.

questions.stem: In 227 BCE Jing Ke tried to kill the king of Qin. He was sent by:
options: Confucian scholars angered by the burning of books
Crown Prince Dan of Yan, who hid a dagger in a map
Lu Buwei, who wanted to rule Qin through the queen
the king of Qi, who feared that Qi would be next
questions.explanation: Jing Ke came offering a map of Yan territory, with a dagger rolled inside it, and narrowly failed. Qin conquered Yan soon afterwards.

questions.stem: Zhang Liang, from a noble family of the former state of Han, arranged an attack on the emperor's convoy at Bolangsha in 218 BCE. The attempt failed because:
options: the strongman's heavy weapon struck the wrong carriage
Meng Tian discovered the plot and arrested the attackers
the emperor had already died and the convoy was empty
the attackers were bribed by Li Si to abandon the plan
questions.explanation: The Shiji says the strongman hit a following carriage, and Zhang Liang escaped. He later became a leading adviser to Liu Bang, founder of the Han.

questions.stem: What do the repeated attempts on the First Emperor's life suggest about his rule?
options: Bitter hostility to Qin survived among the elites of the conquered states
The Qin court was loyal, so all plots came from foreign rulers abroad
The emperor had no fear of attack and travelled without guards
Ordinary peasants were the main supporters of the old Zhou order
questions.explanation: Agents of Yan and nobles of Han such as Zhang Liang sought revenge for the loss of their states. This resentment helps explain the speed of revolt after his death.

questions.stem: When the First Emperor died at Shaqiu during his last tour in 210 BCE, the Shiji says his death was kept secret. How was this done?
options: His officials carried on as normal and a cart of salted fish hid the smell
His son Fusu announced that the emperor had gone into seclusion
His body was taken by sea to the capital while a double rode in his carriage
The court said he had become an immortal and ascended to heaven
questions.explanation: Zhao Gao and Li Si kept up the emperor's routine, with meals and reports sent to his closed carriage, and a load of salted fish masked the smell of decay on the journey.

questions.stem: The Qin dynasty fell in 206 BCE, only four years after the First Emperor's death. Which judgement of his responsibility is most defensible?
options: His harsh rule bred resentment, but his successors sped the collapse
He alone caused the fall, since the Second Emperor reversed all his policies
He bore no responsibility, since the fall was caused only by floods
The fall was caused by a Xiongnu invasion that he had failed to foresee
questions.explanation: Heavy labour and military service, harsh laws and the suppression of the old elites built resentment, but the forged succession and the misrule of Zhao Gao and Huhai turned unrest into collapse.

questions.stem: The Han writer Jia Yi, in 'The Faults of Qin', argued that Qin fell because it:
options: built too few roads to move its troops against the rebels
failed to rule with humaneness and righteousness after conquest
relied too much on Confucian scholars and too little on its army
was too generous to the defeated states and their nobility
questions.explanation: Jia Yi contrasted Qin's power with its swift fall, concluding that a state won by force had to be held by humane rule. His essay shaped the Han view of Qin as a warning.

questions.stem: In the 1970s Chinese Communist Party campaigns praised the First Emperor and the Legalists while attacking Confucius. What does this show about interpretations of Qin Shi Huangdi?
options: Modern historians have proved that every Han account of him was false
The Party discovered new sources that ended all debate about his reign
Admiration for him has always been the official view in China
His image has been reshaped to suit the politics of later eras
questions.explanation: For two thousand years the Confucian tradition condemned him, while Mao and the 1970s campaigns celebrated him as a unifier who crushed reactionary scholars. Each image reflected its own time.

questions.stem: Bamboo slips found in 1975 in the tomb of a Qin official at Shuihudi contain Qin legal and administrative texts, with many fines set in suits of armour or shields. How do they change the picture drawn from the Shiji?
options: They prove that Qin had no written laws and ruled by decree alone
They show that the Qin laws were copied from those of the Zhou kings
They confirm every story of cruelty told about the First Emperor
They show a detailed, bureaucratic legal system, not mere cruelty
questions.explanation: The slips reveal careful rules on procedure, labour and punishment, giving an insider's view of Qin government that balances the hostile Han histories. Harsh punishments do appear, but within an organised system.
